title: Spots on the palms

clues.t: 29-year-old man with a rash on his chest and back for two weeks. It doesn’t itch.
He’s also had fevers, aches and swollen glands.
The rash has spread to his palms and the soles of his feet.
About two months ago he had a painless sore on his penis that healed by itself.
His hair is coming out in small patches, leaving a moth-eaten look.
RPR positive · TPPA positive

pearl: Syphilis has risen sharply in Australia over the past decade, along with cases in babies born to mothers who weren’t diagnosed in time. It’s treated with benzathine penicillin, and anyone tested for syphilis should be offered an HIV test too, and vice versa. On World AIDS Day, the message is the same: test, treat, and talk about it.

title: The thinner's revenge

clues.t: 66-year-old man, six days after heart bypass surgery.
He was recovering well until his left leg swelled and began to ache.
Ultrasound: deep vein clot in the leg, despite blood-thinning
Platelets 88 ×10⁹/L, down from 210 after surgery
The perfusionist's bypass circuit and every injection since have shared one drug.
Antibodies against platelet factor 4: positive

pearl: A platelet fall of more than half, 5 to 10 days into treatment, with new clots rather than bleeding. The paradox is the point: the drug meant to prevent clots is now causing them, so it must be stopped and replaced.

title: Her normal, not yours

clues.t: 33-year-old woman, a wheelchair racer training for her national team.
A pounding headache has come on within minutes.
Her face is flushed and sweaty, but her legs are cool and pale.
She has a complete T4 spinal cord injury from a crash in her teens.
BP 196/104. Her usual is 95/60.
Her catheter bag has been empty for hours. There's a kink in the tube.

pearl: In injuries at T6 or above, anything irritating below the injury can send blood pressure soaring, most often a full bladder. Numbers that look ordinary can be dangerous for someone whose baseline is low. Many people carry a card explaining it, because they often know more about it than the clinician.

title: Red-lining

clues.t: 19-year-old woman, fit and well, collapses 400 m from the end of a charity fun run on a humid morning.
She is agitated, doesn't know where she is, then has a brief seizure.
Her skin is hot and still wet with sweat.
HR 150 · BP 88/50 · glucose 6.1 mmol/L
CK 8,400 U/L · creatinine 190 µmol/L · ALT 310 U/L
Rectal temperature: 41.3 °C

pearl: Classic heat stroke tends to hit older people in heatwaves. The exertional kind strikes fit young people mid-effort, and the sweat fools people: dry skin is not required for the diagnosis.

title: Flood relief

clues.t: 57-year-old woman with fever, cough and rigors for 5 days.
She has type 2 diabetes.
Chest X-ray: upper lobe consolidation
She lives near Darwin and spent the monsoon week volunteering on a flood clean-up, knee-deep in mud.
CT: multiple small abscesses in the liver and spleen
Blood culture: gram-negative bacillus with a "safety pin" look

pearl: It lives in soil and water across South-East Asia and tropical northern Australia, and peaks in the wet season. Diabetes is the biggest risk factor. Rates are several times higher in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, especially in remote communities. Standard pneumonia antibiotics may miss it, so tell the lab when you suspect it.

title: Lattice work
accept: familial amyloidosis of the finnish type

clues.t: 52-year-old woman with dry, gritty eyes for twenty years.
Her optometrist sees fine branching lines across both corneas.
In her forties, her brow and cheeks began to sag on both sides.
Her skin now hangs in loose folds and bruises easily. Her feet are going numb.
Her father and brother have the same face and the same eyes.
Skin biopsy: Congo red-positive deposits. The family comes from south-east Finland.

pearl: First described by Finnish ophthalmologist Jouko Meretoja in 1969, it's one of the 'Finnish disease heritage' conditions. A faulty form of the protein gelsolin folds into amyloid in the cornea, nerves and skin. It's autosomal dominant, and most known cases are Finnish.

title: Seats upright

clues.t: 27-year-old woman with a head cold, flying home for the holidays.
Cruising was uneventful, apart from a blocked nose.
As the plane began to come down, pain built sharply in her right ear.
Swallowing and yawning didn't help at all.
The ear still feels full and muffled after landing.
Otoscopy: red, pulled-in eardrum with fluid behind it

pearl: Cabin pressure rises on the way down, and a Eustachian tube blocked by a cold can't let air in to balance it. That's why descent hurts more than take-off, and why babies do better feeding as the plane descends.

title: Bottle service

clues.t: 2-year-old girl. Her dad has noticed brown marks on her top front teeth.
Her bottom front teeth look perfectly fine.
She falls asleep with a bottle every night.
Usually juice, sometimes milk.
The town's water supply isn't fluoridated.
Her upper front teeth have started to chip and break down.

pearl: The tongue and saliva protect the lower front teeth, so the pattern is the giveaway. Tooth decay is one of the most common chronic diseases of childhood worldwide, and a first dental visit by the first birthday is widely advised.

title: Little visitors

clues.t: 84-year-old woman, sharp as a tack and living independently.
She keeps seeing tiny people in old-fashioned costume on her living-room rug.
They are silent and vivid, and they ignore her completely.
She knows they aren't real, and hasn't told anyone in case they think she's losing her mind.
Cognitive screen 29/30. No delirium. No new medicines.
She has advanced macular degeneration in both eyes.

pearl: When vision fades, the brain's visual areas can start filling in the blanks. In 1760 Charles Bonnet described his own grandfather, Charles Lullin, who was nearly blind and saw patterns, people and carriages. Oliver Sacks wrote warmly about it. Asking kindly matters, because people often hide it for fear of being called demented.

title: Not the stress

clues.t: 45-year-old woman with gnawing upper abdominal pain that wakes her at 2 am.
Food and a glass of milk ease it for a while.
She blames her stressful job. So did her last doctor.
Hb 112 g/L · MCV 78 fL
Gastroscopy: clean-based crater in the first part of the duodenum
Urea breath test positive. Biopsy shows curved Gram-negative rods.

pearl: Stress got the blame for decades. In Perth, Robin Warren and Barry Marshall showed a bacterium was behind most ulcers, and Marshall drank a culture of it in 1984 to help prove the point. They shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

title: The slow climber
accept: high altitude oedema of the lung

clues.t: 36-year-old man, a marathon runner, on day three of a fast Himalayan trek.
Today he keeps falling behind. His pack feels twice as heavy.
A dry cough kept him up all night.
He's breathless just sitting on his bunk. His lips look dusky.
SpO₂ 62% at 4,300 m · crackles at both lung bases
He has started coughing up pink, frothy sputum.

pearl: Fitness offers no protection. Low oxygen clamps the lung's blood vessels unevenly, and the high-pressure patches leak. It's the leading cause of death from altitude illness, it can come without the classic headache, and descending promptly is the key treatment.

title: A childhood sore throat

clues.t: 24-year-old woman, 28 weeks pregnant, more breathless each week.
She now sleeps sitting up on three pillows.
She grew up in a crowded house in a remote community, and clinic visits were a day's travel away.
At age 9 she had painful swollen joints that moved from knee to ankle to elbow.
A loud first heart sound, then a low rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex.
Echo: thickened, fused valve leaflets with a 'hockey stick' shape opening

pearl: A disease of poverty, not bad luck. It follows untreated strep infections, is linked to crowding, and has nearly vanished from wealthy settings but remains common in low-income countries and in Aboriginal, Māori and Pacific communities. Pregnancy's extra blood volume often unmasks it.

title: Normal at rest

clues.t: 13-year-old girl who has fainted three times this year.
Twice in the pool, once when a friend jumped out at her.
She was told she had epilepsy, but the tablets changed nothing.
Resting ECG and echo: normal
She collapses at training. A coach uses the club's defibrillator: VF, one shock, pulse back.
Exercise test: at HR 130 the QRS alternates direction, beat by beat. Her cousin drowned at 11, a strong swimmer.

pearl: Adrenaline makes heart cells mishandle calcium, usually through an RYR2 variant, so a normal resting ECG is the trap. Fainting during exercise or fright is never 'just a faint' until the heart is cleared. Claude Beck's first human defibrillation, in 1947, saved a 14-year-old.

title: Leaning in

clues.t: 44-year-old man with the worst sore throat of his life, come on over a few hours.
He can't swallow his own saliva and is spitting into a tissue.
His voice sounds as though he's talking through a hot potato.
He's sitting bolt upright, leaning forward on his hands with his chin pushed out.
Temp 39.4°C · a high-pitched noise when he breathes in
Lateral neck X-ray: a swollen 'thumb' above the airway

pearl: The Hib vaccine has made it far rarer in children, so adults are now a larger share of cases. George Washington's fatal throat illness in 1799 is often put down to it. His doctors, doing their best by the standards of the day, drew off a large share of his blood.

title: Lights out

clues.t: 68-year-old woman watching a film in a dark cinema.
Suddenly, severe pain in her right eye and forehead.
She sees rainbow haloes around the exit lights.
She starts vomiting, and her family assume it's something she ate.
Her right eye is red and the pupil is mid-sized and doesn't react.
The eye feels rock-hard through the closed lid.

pearl: Dim light widens the pupil, and in a narrow eye that can shut the drainage angle. Pressure soars within hours, and sight is at stake, so this is an emergency. On Zamenhof Day, a nod to the Polish eye doctor who also invented Esperanto.

title: Better at the pub

clues.t: 32-year-old woman whose hearing has been slowly fading in both ears.
Oddly, she follows conversation better in a noisy pub than a quiet room.
Her mother needed hearing aids young.
It got noticeably worse during her pregnancy.
Both eardrums look completely normal.
Audiogram: conductive loss, with a bone-conduction dip at 2 kHz

pearl: Abnormal bone growth fixes the stapes in place. Hearing better in noise is called paracusis of Willis, and the 2 kHz dip is the Carhart notch. Otosclerosis is one of many theories for Beethoven's deafness, and the true cause has never been settled.

title: Cabin pressure

clues.t: 38-year-old man on a flight home from a tropical holiday. A deep ache has started in his right shoulder.
By landing, his legs tingle and feel heavy, and his thinking is foggy.
A blotchy, marbled rash has appeared across his chest.
ECG, troponin and D-dimer: all normal
He did his last deep scuba dive the morning before he flew.
He improves on 100% oxygen. The hospital calls the hyperbaric unit.

pearl: Airliner cabins are pressurised only to about 2,400 m, which is enough for leftover nitrogen from a dive to bubble out of the tissues. Dive agencies advise waiting 12 to 24 hours before flying, longer after multiple dives.

title: A long way from home

clues.t: 46-year-old cleaner who tires easily and gets breathless on the stairs.
She has fainted twice in the past month.
She moved to Madrid from rural Bolivia 12 years ago. As a girl she slept in an adobe house with a thatched roof.
ECG: right bundle branch block plus left anterior fascicular block
Echo: apical left ventricular aneurysm, ejection fraction 35%
IgG positive on two different serological tests for a protozoan spread by triatomine bugs

pearl: Carlos Chagas described the disease in Brazil in 1909: parasite, insect vector and first patient, a two-year-old girl called Berenice. With migration it is now seen well beyond Latin America, including in Europe, and it can pass from mother to baby in pregnancy.

title: The King's Evil

clues.t: 8-year-old girl with a painless lump on the side of her neck, there for two months.
A course of antibiotics did nothing.
The lump is now firm and matted, and the skin over it has turned purplish.
Her grandfather, who stayed with the family last year, had a cough that lasted for months.
Fine-needle aspirate: caseating granulomas
Ziehl-Neelsen stain: acid-fast bacilli

pearl: Common in Victorian Britain, often thanks to unpasteurised milk. For centuries English and French monarchs were believed to cure it with a touch: the writer Samuel Johnson was touched by Queen Anne as a small child. It didn't work.

title: Common ground

clues.t: 40-year-old woman, a farmer, with heavy, itchy feet since her teens.
Both legs have slowly swollen, always below the knee.
The skin of her feet has thickened, with moss-like bumps.
Blood tests for filarial worm infection: negative. No mosquito-borne cause found.
She has worked barefoot her whole life on red volcanic clay in the Ethiopian highlands.
Many of her neighbours have it too. Their children who wear shoes don't.

pearl: Mineral particles from irritant volcanic soil enter through the skin of bare feet and inflame the lymphatics in people with a genetic susceptibility. WHO estimates about 1 million people are affected in Ethiopia alone. It is entirely preventable with shoes and clean floors, yet it brings heavy stigma.

title: Deep breaths

clues.t: 20-year-old woman giving blood for the first time.
She feels hot, clammy and sick, and her vision narrows to a tunnel.
She slumps in the chair and is out for about 15 seconds.
She comes round quickly and clear-headed. No tongue bite.
HR 44 · BP 82/48, both recovering within minutes
It happened once before, at the sight of her brother's stitches.

pearl: A surge through the vagus nerve slows the heart and relaxes the blood vessels. The word vagus means 'wandering', since the nerve travels from the brainstem to the gut. Tensing the leg and arm muscles at the first warning can head a faint off.

title: Hark, the herald

clues.t: 19-year-old woman with a new rash on her trunk.
It began a week ago with one oval pink patch, which she took for ringworm.
Now dozens of smaller patches have joined it.
Each has a fine collar of scale just inside its edge.
Only mildly itchy. She feels completely well.
On her back, the patches slope down and out like the branches of a Christmas tree.

pearl: The first patch is the 'herald' that announces the rest. Reactivated herpesviruses 6 and 7 are suspected but not proven as the cause. It usually fades by itself within a couple of months, and antifungal cream does nothing for it.

title: Runs in the family

clues.t: 38-year-old man with high blood pressure since his late twenties.
Dull flank pain on and off, and pink urine once after a hard game of football.
eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m²
His mother started dialysis at 54, then had a transplant from her brother.
His doctor can feel a large mass in each flank.
Ultrasound: both kidneys huge and riddled with fluid-filled sacs, with more in the liver

pearl: The most common inherited kidney disease, usually from PKD1 or PKD2 variants. Brain aneurysms run in some families, so family history matters. The first successful kidney transplant was between identical twins, Ronald and Richard Herrick, in Boston on 23 December 1954.

title: Stocking filler

clues.t: 18-month-old girl, drooling and refusing her Christmas Eve dinner.
She was well an hour ago. Now she's gagging and coughing on and off.
Her voice has gone hoarse.
A musical greeting card on the coffee table has been pulled apart.
Chest X-ray: round metallic object in the upper oesophagus
Close up: a double ring at its edge on the front view, a step on the side view

pearl: Happy birthday James Joule: a small cell holds plenty of energy. Against a wet oesophageal wall it sets up a current that makes caustic hydroxide, and serious burns can start within 2 hours. A coin looks similar, which is why the 'halo' is worth looking for. This one is always an emergency.

title: 'Tis the season

clues.t: 38-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department on Christmas night saying her heart is flopping like a fish in her chest.
No heart history, no regular medicines, two children, one tired partner.
It's her third party in three days, after work drinks on Monday.
HR 138, irregularly irregular · BP 122/76
Echo: normal · TSH: normal · Troponin: not raised
Back in normal rhythm by the next morning.

pearl: Named by Philip Ettinger and colleagues in 1978, after drinkers with no known heart disease turned up with rhythm problems following weekends and holidays. Usually it's atrial fibrillation, and it often settles by itself, but that doesn't make it a Christmas tradition.

title: Strike a light
answer: Phossy jaw (phosphorus necrosis of the jaw)

clues.t: 19-year-old woman in East London, 1888, with toothache and a swollen face.
An abscess in her jaw keeps discharging, and it smells foul.
Her dentist pulled a tooth. Now bare bone is showing through her gum.
Some say the diseased bone glows faintly in the dark.
At work she dips sticks into a paste all day, breathing its fumes.
This summer, she and her workmates walked out on strike over pay, fines and conditions.

pearl: Caused by white phosphorus fumes in match factories. The 1888 Bryant & May matchgirls’ strike helped expose it, and the 1906 Berne Convention banned white phosphorus in matches. Its modern cousin is medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, seen with bisphosphonates. A century ago, the Radium Girls faced a strikingly similar jaw disease.

title: Everyone had flu that year

clues.t: 23-year-old woman in Vienna, 1919, with sore throat, fever and headache.
Her doctor assumes it's the same influenza as everyone else.
Then she develops double vision, and her eyes stop moving properly.
She sleeps up to 20 hours a day, wakes when spoken to, answers sensibly, and drops off again.
Hospitals across Europe and beyond are seeing the same strange cases.
Years later she freezes in place, as if with severe parkinsonism.

pearl: Constantin von Economo described it in Vienna in 1917, and it spread worldwide until about 1928, then all but vanished. The cause has never been established. Decades later, Oliver Sacks gave survivors levodopa in New York, the story behind his book Awakenings.

title: Origin story

clues.t: 17-year-old woman, her school's star volleyball player, and much taller and slimmer than anyone in her family bar her father.
Her arm span is longer than her height.
Her breastbone sticks outward.
The lens in one of her eyes has shifted out of place.
Gripping her own wrist, her thumb and little finger overlap easily.
Echo: widened aortic root

pearl: Named after French paediatrician Antoine Marfan, who described a tall, long-limbed girl in 1896. A variant in FBN1 weakens connective tissue. Real biology offers no superpowers here, but regular aortic monitoring has transformed life expectancy.

title: Bounces back

clues.t: 29-year-old woman who has needed iron infusions every six months since her teens.
Two sets of scopes found only 'a few small bruise-like spots', nothing worth treating.
A tender spot on the sole of her foot has been blamed on her shoes for years.
Close up, it's a soft dark dome. It flattens when pressed, then slowly refills.
Capsule endoscopy: dozens of violet, nipple-like lesions through the small bowel
Biopsy: thin-walled venous channels. Sequencing of the lesion finds a TEK (TIE2) variant.

pearl: Happy birthday Charles Goodyear. Rare venous malformations in the skin and gut, named by William Bean in 1958 for their rubbery feel. Most cases are sporadic, and the gut lesions cause chronic bleeding. Sirolimus has shown promise in reports of individual patients.

title: Red flag on the ninth

clues.t: 46-year-old man, a keen golfer, with low back pain since one big swing.
Now the pain is shooting down both legs.
He can't feel the toilet paper when he wipes.
He can't tell when he's passing urine.
Post-void bladder scan: 780 mL
MRI: large central L4/5 disc squashing the bundle of nerve roots below the spinal cord

pearl: Most back pain settles, and this is the rare exception that can't wait. Pain in both legs, saddle numbness, and bladder, bowel or sexual changes need same-day assessment, because delays can mean permanent loss of function.

title: After the countdown

clues.t: 27-year-old woman at a New Year’s Eve party. The champagne went down well, then came back up.
Repeated retching and vomiting, just after midnight.
On the fifth go, streaks of bright red blood in the vomit.
No chest pain. No trouble swallowing. Nothing crackles under the skin of her neck.
Endoscopy: a short linear split in the lining at the gastro-oesophageal junction, no longer bleeding

pearl: A tear through the lining only, usually from forceful retching. Most stop bleeding on their own. Mallory and Weiss described it in 1929 after alcohol binges. Its dangerous cousin, Boerhaave syndrome, goes right through the wall; Herman Boerhaave was born on this day in 1668.
